changes.change: Offer every champion facing a CFO who won't meet us a one-page business case built on their own numbers: their failed-order rate from their own dashboard (for example 'one in twelve online orders'), what those failed orders are worth from a three-month export, and the cost their current processor can't explain. Offer it before pricing goes out, and treat a champion's request for something to hand the CFO as a must-answer.
changes.why: The champion asked for a one-page business case to hand the CFO, we sent the deck and pricing proposal, and the decline analysis was dropped, so the decider saw only the controller's page.

changes.current_line: Customers see an average uplift in authorization rates with Authorization Boost and Adaptive Acceptance.
changes.change: Stop 'orders dying at the last step', especially 'the big baskets'. Here is why your big orders get declined, and what your declined orders are worth. Use this with buyers who bring us a checkout-failure problem, and put their own decline figure in place of the average.
changes.why: The specific explanation of why big orders fail landed with the champion, the average-uplift slide did nothing for the decider, and the customer described the problem as 'orders dying at the last step' and 'the big baskets'.

changes.change: When an incumbent counters on rate, don't negotiate the rate line alone. Answer with the decline cost the incumbent can't explain: a better rate still applies to orders that keep failing. Every pricing proposal should show rate next to total cost and recovered revenue (failed orders, gateway fee, chargeback handling), so a side-by-side can't read as 'the same thing'.
changes.why: After the bank sharpened its rate, every email was about rate, and the deciding page compared only rates, so the CFO read us as 'the same thing'. The rep concedes a matched rate still left no reason to move.

changes.current_line: Financial infrastructure to grow globally, in every currency.
changes.change: For buyers who come to us because checkouts are failing, open with the cost of those failures instead of global growth: 'we do all the work to get someone to buy a four-thousand-dollar greenhouse and then the card says no'. What are your failed orders worth, and why can't your processor tell you?
changes.why: The deal started with a measured failed-order rate from the customer's own dashboard and a processor that couldn't explain it, not with any interest in global reach.
